Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2

R
ggplot2
Data Visualization
Treemap
Tutorial
A step-by-step guide to building treemaps from basic to advanced, perfect for visualizing hierarchical data
Author

Joao Luiz D’Andrea

Published

October 12, 2025

Introduction

Treemaps are excellent for visualizing hierarchical data and proportions. They display data as nested rectangles, where the size of each rectangle represents a quantitative value. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated treemaps using ggplot2 and the treemapify package.

We’ll analyze the distribution of car manufacturers and their fuel efficiency using the built-in mpg dataset.

Setup

First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(treemapify)     # For creating treemaps with ggplot2
library(scales)         # For formatting labels

# Prepare the data: summarize by manufacturer
data_summary <- mpg %>%
  group_by(manufacturer) %>%                        # Group by car manufacturer
  summarise(
    count = n(),                                    # Count number of models
    avg_hwy = mean(hwy),                           # Average highway mpg
    avg_cty = mean(cty)                            # Average city mpg
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(count))                              # Sort by count (highest to lowest)

# Preview the data
head(data_summary, 10)
# A tibble: 10 × 4
   manufacturer count avg_hwy avg_cty
   <chr>        <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 dodge           37    17.9    13.1
 2 toyota          34    24.9    18.5
 3 volkswagen      27    29.2    20.9
 4 ford            25    19.4    14  
 5 chevrolet       19    21.9    15  
 6 audi            18    26.4    17.6
 7 hyundai         14    26.9    18.6
 8 subaru          14    25.6    19.3
 9 nissan          13    24.6    18.1
10 honda            9    32.6    24.4

Chart 1: Basic Treemap

Let’s start with a simple treemap showing the number of car models per manufacturer.

ggplot(data_summary, aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer)) +  # Set area size and fill color
  geom_treemap()                                                  # Create treemap

Code Explanation

Line 1: ggplot(data_summary, aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer)) - Initializes the treemap with area representing the number of models (rectangle size) and fill assigning different colors to each manufacturer

Line 2: geom_treemap() - Creates the treemap layout, automatically calculating rectangle positions and sizes based on the area values

What we have so far: A functional treemap showing proportions, but it’s hard to identify which rectangle represents which manufacturer. The colors are randomly assigned and there’s no context.

Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement

Now we’ll add labels, improve the color scheme, and provide context through titles and better formatting.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

  • Manufacturer labels inside each rectangle for identification
  • Model count labels to show exact values
  • Custom color palette for better visual appeal
  • Title and subtitle to provide context
  • Cleaner theme with better spacing
  • Label sizing based on rectangle area for readability
ggplot(data_summary, aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer, label = manufacturer)) +
  geom_treemap() +                                                # Create treemap rectangles
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white",                                             # White text for contrast
    place = "centre",                                             # Center the text
    size = 12,                                                    # Base text size
    grow = TRUE                                                   # Auto-size text to fit rectangles
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    aes(label = paste0("n=", count)),                            # Add count labels
    colour = "white",                                             # White text
    place = "bottom",                                             # Position at bottom of rectangle
    size = 10,                                                    # Slightly smaller text
    alpha = 0.8                                                   # Slight transparency
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma") +                      # Use viridis color palette
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Car Models by Manufacturer",         # Main title
    subtitle = "Based on EPA fuel economy dataset (1999-2008)",   # Context subtitle
    caption = "Rectangle size represents number of car models"    # Explain the visual encoding
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                               # Clean theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    legend.position = "none",                                     # Remove legend (redundant with labels)
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)                         # Add margins around plot
  )

Code Explanation

Line 1: aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer, label = manufacturer) - Added label aesthetic to prepare for text labels

Line 2: geom_treemap() - Creates the base treemap rectangles

Lines 3-8: First geom_treemap_text() layer - Adds manufacturer names in white, centered, with grow = TRUE which automatically scales text to fit within each rectangle

Lines 9-15: Second geom_treemap_text() layer - Adds model counts at the bottom of each rectangle with “n=” prefix for clarity

Line 16: scale_fill_viridis_d() - Applies a colorblind-friendly viridis palette (discrete version) for better accessibility and visual appeal

Lines 17-21: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle providing context, and caption explaining what rectangle size represents

Lines 22-28: Theme customization - Removes the legend (since labels identify each manufacturer), styles the title and subtitle, and adds proper margins

What we have now: A much more informative treemap with clear labels identifying each manufacturer and showing exact counts. The color palette is visually appealing and accessible, and the context is provided through proper labeling.

Chart 3: Advanced Visualization

Let’s create a sophisticated treemap that shows both quantity and quality (fuel efficiency) through size and color, with enhanced styling.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

  • Color mapping to fuel efficiency - Rectangle color now represents average highway MPG (dual encoding)
  • Custom gradient color scale - Low efficiency (red) to high efficiency (green)
  • Borders around rectangles - Better visual separation
  • Enhanced label formatting - Shows both manufacturer and efficiency
  • Legend with custom formatting - Clear explanation of color meaning
  • Professional styling - Publication-ready appearance
  • Data insight annotation - Highlights key findings in subtitle
# Add efficiency categories for better interpretation
data_summary <- data_summary %>%
  mutate(
    efficiency_category = case_when(                   # Create categorical labels
      avg_hwy >= 25 ~ "High Efficiency",              # High performers
      avg_hwy >= 20 ~ "Medium Efficiency",            # Average performers
      TRUE ~ "Lower Efficiency"                       # Below average
    )
  )

ggplot(data_summary, aes(
  area = count, 
  fill = avg_hwy,                                     # Color by fuel efficiency
  label = manufacturer, 
  subgroup = efficiency_category                      # Group by efficiency level
)) +
  geom_treemap(
    colour = "white",                                 # White borders between rectangles
    size = 2                                          # Border thickness
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white",                                 # White text for visibility
    place = "centre",                                 # Center manufacturer name
    size = 14,                                        # Larger base size
    grow = TRUE,                                      # Auto-scale to fit
    fontface = "bold",                                # Bold text for emphasis
    alpha = 0.9                                       # Slight transparency
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    aes(label = paste0(count, " models\n", 
                       round(avg_hwy, 1), " mpg")),   # Multi-line label with count and efficiency
    colour = "white",                                 # White text
    place = "bottom",                                 # Position at bottom
    size = 10,                                        # Smaller for secondary info
    alpha = 0.7,                                      # More transparent
    lineheight = 0.9                                  # Tighter line spacing
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",                                  # Red for low efficiency
    mid = "#F4A261",                                  # Orange for medium
    high = "#52A675",                                 # Green for high efficiency
    midpoint = 22,                                    # Set midpoint of scale
    name = "Average Highway\nFuel Efficiency",        # Legend title
    breaks = seq(15, 30, by = 5),                     # Legend breaks
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg"),           # Add units to legend
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      barwidth = 15,                                  # Wider color bar
      barheight = 0.8,                                # Thinner bar
      title.position = "top",                         # Title above bar
      title.hjust = 0.5                               # Center the title
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Car Manufacturers: Market Presence vs. Fuel Efficiency",
    subtitle = "Dodge leads in model count (37 models) but lags in fuel efficiency (17.9 mpg)\nVolkswagen and Honda balance quantity with quality (29.2 and 28.8 mpg respectively)",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008) | Rectangle size = number of models | Color = average highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +                     # Clean base theme with larger font
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold", 
      size = 18, 
      hjust = 0.5,                                    # Center the title
      margin = margin(b = 10)
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11, 
      color = "#5A6C7D", 
      hjust = 0.5,                                    # Center subtitle
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2                                # Better line spacing for multi-line
    ),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9, 
      color = "#6C757D", 
      hjust = 0.5,                                    # Center caption
      margin = margin(t = 20)
    ),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",                       # Place legend at bottom
    legend.title = element_text(
      face = "bold", 
      size = 11
    ),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.margin = margin(t = 15),                   # Space between plot and legend
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(
      fill = "white", 
      colour = NA
    ),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),            # Generous margins
    
    # Remove grid (not needed for treemap)
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

Code Explanation

Lines 2-10: Creates an efficiency_category variable to group manufacturers into high/medium/lower efficiency brackets for potential subgrouping

Lines 12-17: Enhanced aes() mapping: - area = count - Rectangle size by model count - fill = avg_hwy - Color by fuel efficiency (continuous scale) - label = manufacturer - Manufacturer names - subgroup = efficiency_category - Groups for potential hierarchical organization

Lines 18-21: geom_treemap() with white borders (2px width) to clearly separate rectangles and improve readability

Lines 22-29: First text layer with bold, white manufacturer names that automatically scale to fit rectangles

Lines 30-38: Second text layer showing both model count and fuel efficiency in a compact two-line format at the bottom of each rectangle

Lines 39-52: scale_fill_gradient2() - Creates a diverging color scale: - Red for poor efficiency, green for good efficiency - Midpoint set at 22 mpg (approximate average) - Custom legend with formatted labels including “mpg” units - Horizontal color bar for better space usage

Lines 53-57: Comprehensive labels with: - Clear title explaining both dimensions (size and color) - Data-driven subtitle highlighting key insights - Detailed caption explaining all encodings

Lines 58-95: Extensive theme customization: - Centered titles and captions for balanced layout - Larger base font size for better readability - Professional spacing and margins - Customized legend placement and styling - Removed grid (unnecessary for treemaps)

Final result: A publication-ready treemap that tells a complete story. Viewers can instantly see both market presence (size) and fuel efficiency performance (color), with clear labels and professional styling. The dual encoding reveals patterns like Dodge’s high model count but poor efficiency, while Honda balances both aspects well.

Comparison: All Three Charts

Here’s how our treemaps evolved:

Aspect Basic Intermediate Advanced
Identifiability Poor (no labels) Good (clear labels) Excellent (labels + data values)
Information Density Low (only size) Medium (size + names) High (size + efficiency + context)
Color Purpose Random distinction Aesthetic only Meaningful (efficiency encoding)
Context None Basic title Full story with insights
Visual Quality Basic Improved Publication-ready
Data Dimensions 1 (count only) 1 (count only) 2 (count + efficiency)

When to Use Treemaps

Treemaps work best for:

✅ Showing proportions - Quickly compare relative sizes of categories

✅ Hierarchical data - Display parent-child relationships (we can add subgroups)

✅ Part-to-whole relationships - See how individual parts make up a total

✅ Limited categories - Work best with 10-20 categories (more becomes cluttered)

✅ Dual encoding - Show two variables simultaneously (size + color)

Avoid treemaps when:

❌ Precise value comparison is critical (use bar charts)

❌ Data changes over time (use line charts)

❌ Too many small categories (creates tiny, unreadable rectangles)

❌ Negative values are present (treemaps require positive values)

Key Takeaways

Tips for Creating Better Treemaps:

  1. Always add labels - Use geom_treemap_text() to identify rectangles. Unlabeled treemaps are nearly useless

  2. Use color meaningfully - Don’t just use color for distinction; map it to a second variable (like efficiency, growth rate, or category)

  3. Consider borders - White borders between rectangles improve clarity and prevent colors from bleeding together

  4. Limit your categories - If you have too many categories, group smaller ones into “Other” to maintain readability

  5. Use grow = TRUE - This makes text automatically resize to fit rectangles, ensuring readability for all sizes

  6. Choose appropriate color scales:

    • Sequential (light to dark) for continuous positive values
    • Diverging (red-white-green) when there’s a meaningful midpoint
    • Categorical for distinct groups

  7. Add multiple text layers - Use separate layers for main labels and supporting information (like our count + efficiency example)

  8. Test text contrast - Ensure text is readable against all background colors. White text with slight transparency often works well

  9. Include a legend - When color encodes data, always include a properly labeled legend explaining what it represents

  10. Provide context in subtitles - Don’t just show the data; highlight key insights or patterns in your subtitle

  11. Sort your data - Arrange categories by size (descending) before creating the treemap for better visual organization

  12. Consider hierarchical treemaps - Use the subgroup parameter to create nested treemaps for multi-level hierarchies

Advanced: Hierarchical Treemap Example

Want to show multiple levels of hierarchy? Here’s a bonus example with manufacturers grouped by country:

# Add country information (simplified example)
data_hierarchical <- mpg %>%
  mutate(
    country = case_when(
      manufacturer %in% c("audi", "volkswagen") ~ "Germany",
      manufacturer %in% c("toyota", "honda", "nissan", "subaru") ~ "Japan",
      manufacturer %in% c("hyundai") ~ "South Korea",
      TRUE ~ "USA"
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(country, manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(count = n(), avg_hwy = mean(hwy), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(data_hierarchical, aes(
  area = count,
  fill = avg_hwy,
  label = manufacturer,
  subgroup = country                      # Group by country first
)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(          # Add borders around country groups
    colour = "white",
    size = 4
  ) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_text(            # Add country labels
    place = "centre",
    colour = "white",
    alpha = 0.7,
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 16
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(                     # Add manufacturer labels
    colour = "white",
    place = "centre",
    size = 10,
    grow = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",
    mid = "#F4A261",
    high = "#52A675",
    midpoint = 22,
    name = "Avg Highway MPG"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Car Models by Country and Manufacturer",
    subtitle = "Hierarchical view showing country-level groupings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5)
  )

Alternative Packages

While we used treemapify in this tutorial, here are other options:

  • treemap - More traditional treemap package with different layout algorithms
  • d3treeR - Interactive treemaps using D3.js (great for Shiny apps!)
  • plotly - Can create interactive treemaps with hover information

## Introduction

Treemaps are excellent for visualizing hierarchical data and proportions. They display data as nested rectangles, where the size of each rectangle represents a quantitative value. In this tutorial, we'll create increasingly sophisticated treemaps using `ggplot2` and the `treemapify` package.

We'll analyze the distribution of car manufacturers and their fuel efficiency using the built-in `mpg` dataset.

## Setup

First, let's load the required packages and prepare our data:

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(treemapify)     # For creating treemaps with ggplot2
library(scales)         # For formatting labels

# Prepare the data: summarize by manufacturer
data_summary <- mpg %>%
  group_by(manufacturer) %>%                        # Group by car manufacturer
  summarise(
    count = n(),                                    # Count number of models
    avg_hwy = mean(hwy),                           # Average highway mpg
    avg_cty = mean(cty)                            # Average city mpg
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(count))                              # Sort by count (highest to lowest)

# Preview the data
head(data_summary, 10)
```

---

## Chart 1: Basic Treemap

Let's start with a simple treemap showing the number of car models per manufacturer.

```{r}
#| label: chart-basic
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

ggplot(data_summary, aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer)) +  # Set area size and fill color
  geom_treemap()                                                  # Create treemap
```

### Code Explanation

**Line 1:** `ggplot(data_summary, aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer))` - Initializes the treemap with `area` representing the number of models (rectangle size) and `fill` assigning different colors to each manufacturer

**Line 2:** `geom_treemap()` - Creates the treemap layout, automatically calculating rectangle positions and sizes based on the area values

::: {.highlight-box .info}
**What we have so far:**
A functional treemap showing proportions, but it's hard to identify which rectangle represents which manufacturer. The colors are randomly assigned and there's no context.
:::

---

## Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement

Now we'll add labels, improve the color scheme, and provide context through titles and better formatting.

::: {.highlight-box .warning}
**What we're adding in this evolution:**

- **Manufacturer labels** inside each rectangle for identification
- **Model count labels** to show exact values
- **Custom color palette** for better visual appeal
- **Title and subtitle** to provide context
- **Cleaner theme** with better spacing
- **Label sizing** based on rectangle area for readability

:::

```{r}
#| label: chart-intermediate
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

ggplot(data_summary, aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer, label = manufacturer)) +
  geom_treemap() +                                                # Create treemap rectangles
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white",                                             # White text for contrast
    place = "centre",                                             # Center the text
    size = 12,                                                    # Base text size
    grow = TRUE                                                   # Auto-size text to fit rectangles
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    aes(label = paste0("n=", count)),                            # Add count labels
    colour = "white",                                             # White text
    place = "bottom",                                             # Position at bottom of rectangle
    size = 10,                                                    # Slightly smaller text
    alpha = 0.8                                                   # Slight transparency
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma") +                      # Use viridis color palette
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Car Models by Manufacturer",         # Main title
    subtitle = "Based on EPA fuel economy dataset (1999-2008)",   # Context subtitle
    caption = "Rectangle size represents number of car models"    # Explain the visual encoding
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                               # Clean theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    legend.position = "none",                                     # Remove legend (redundant with labels)
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)                         # Add margins around plot
  )
```

### Code Explanation

**Line 1:** `aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer, label = manufacturer)` - Added `label` aesthetic to prepare for text labels

**Line 2:** `geom_treemap()` - Creates the base treemap rectangles

**Lines 3-8:** First `geom_treemap_text()` layer - Adds manufacturer names in white, centered, with `grow = TRUE` which automatically scales text to fit within each rectangle

**Lines 9-15:** Second `geom_treemap_text()` layer - Adds model counts at the bottom of each rectangle with "n=" prefix for clarity

**Line 16:** `scale_fill_viridis_d()` - Applies a colorblind-friendly viridis palette (discrete version) for better accessibility and visual appeal

**Lines 17-21:** `labs()` - Adds descriptive title, subtitle providing context, and caption explaining what rectangle size represents

**Lines 22-28:** Theme customization - Removes the legend (since labels identify each manufacturer), styles the title and subtitle, and adds proper margins

::: {.highlight-box .success}
**What we have now:**
A much more informative treemap with clear labels identifying each manufacturer and showing exact counts. The color palette is visually appealing and accessible, and the context is provided through proper labeling.
:::

---

## Chart 3: Advanced Visualization

Let's create a sophisticated treemap that shows both quantity and quality (fuel efficiency) through size and color, with enhanced styling.

::: {.highlight-box .warning}
**What we're adding in this final evolution:**

- **Color mapping to fuel efficiency** - Rectangle color now represents average highway MPG (dual encoding)
- **Custom gradient color scale** - Low efficiency (red) to high efficiency (green)
- **Borders around rectangles** - Better visual separation
- **Enhanced label formatting** - Shows both manufacturer and efficiency
- **Legend with custom formatting** - Clear explanation of color meaning
- **Professional styling** - Publication-ready appearance
- **Data insight annotation** - Highlights key findings in subtitle

:::

```{r}
#| label: chart-advanced
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8

# Add efficiency categories for better interpretation
data_summary <- data_summary %>%
  mutate(
    efficiency_category = case_when(                   # Create categorical labels
      avg_hwy >= 25 ~ "High Efficiency",              # High performers
      avg_hwy >= 20 ~ "Medium Efficiency",            # Average performers
      TRUE ~ "Lower Efficiency"                       # Below average
    )
  )

ggplot(data_summary, aes(
  area = count, 
  fill = avg_hwy,                                     # Color by fuel efficiency
  label = manufacturer, 
  subgroup = efficiency_category                      # Group by efficiency level
)) +
  geom_treemap(
    colour = "white",                                 # White borders between rectangles
    size = 2                                          # Border thickness
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white",                                 # White text for visibility
    place = "centre",                                 # Center manufacturer name
    size = 14,                                        # Larger base size
    grow = TRUE,                                      # Auto-scale to fit
    fontface = "bold",                                # Bold text for emphasis
    alpha = 0.9                                       # Slight transparency
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    aes(label = paste0(count, " models\n", 
                       round(avg_hwy, 1), " mpg")),   # Multi-line label with count and efficiency
    colour = "white",                                 # White text
    place = "bottom",                                 # Position at bottom
    size = 10,                                        # Smaller for secondary info
    alpha = 0.7,                                      # More transparent
    lineheight = 0.9                                  # Tighter line spacing
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",                                  # Red for low efficiency
    mid = "#F4A261",                                  # Orange for medium
    high = "#52A675",                                 # Green for high efficiency
    midpoint = 22,                                    # Set midpoint of scale
    name = "Average Highway\nFuel Efficiency",        # Legend title
    breaks = seq(15, 30, by = 5),                     # Legend breaks
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg"),           # Add units to legend
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      barwidth = 15,                                  # Wider color bar
      barheight = 0.8,                                # Thinner bar
      title.position = "top",                         # Title above bar
      title.hjust = 0.5                               # Center the title
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Car Manufacturers: Market Presence vs. Fuel Efficiency",
    subtitle = "Dodge leads in model count (37 models) but lags in fuel efficiency (17.9 mpg)\nVolkswagen and Honda balance quantity with quality (29.2 and 28.8 mpg respectively)",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008) | Rectangle size = number of models | Color = average highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +                     # Clean base theme with larger font
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold", 
      size = 18, 
      hjust = 0.5,                                    # Center the title
      margin = margin(b = 10)
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11, 
      color = "#5A6C7D", 
      hjust = 0.5,                                    # Center subtitle
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2                                # Better line spacing for multi-line
    ),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9, 
      color = "#6C757D", 
      hjust = 0.5,                                    # Center caption
      margin = margin(t = 20)
    ),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",                       # Place legend at bottom
    legend.title = element_text(
      face = "bold", 
      size = 11
    ),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.margin = margin(t = 15),                   # Space between plot and legend
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(
      fill = "white", 
      colour = NA
    ),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),            # Generous margins
    
    # Remove grid (not needed for treemap)
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

### Code Explanation

**Lines 2-10:** Creates an `efficiency_category` variable to group manufacturers into high/medium/lower efficiency brackets for potential subgrouping

**Lines 12-17:** Enhanced `aes()` mapping:
- `area = count` - Rectangle size by model count
- `fill = avg_hwy` - Color by fuel efficiency (continuous scale)
- `label = manufacturer` - Manufacturer names
- `subgroup = efficiency_category` - Groups for potential hierarchical organization

**Lines 18-21:** `geom_treemap()` with white borders (2px width) to clearly separate rectangles and improve readability

**Lines 22-29:** First text layer with bold, white manufacturer names that automatically scale to fit rectangles

**Lines 30-38:** Second text layer showing both model count and fuel efficiency in a compact two-line format at the bottom of each rectangle

**Lines 39-52:** `scale_fill_gradient2()` - Creates a diverging color scale:
- Red for poor efficiency, green for good efficiency
- Midpoint set at 22 mpg (approximate average)
- Custom legend with formatted labels including "mpg" units
- Horizontal color bar for better space usage

**Lines 53-57:** Comprehensive labels with:
- Clear title explaining both dimensions (size and color)
- Data-driven subtitle highlighting key insights
- Detailed caption explaining all encodings

**Lines 58-95:** Extensive theme customization:
- Centered titles and captions for balanced layout
- Larger base font size for better readability
- Professional spacing and margins
- Customized legend placement and styling
- Removed grid (unnecessary for treemaps)

::: {.highlight-box .success}
**Final result:**
A publication-ready treemap that tells a complete story. Viewers can instantly see both market presence (size) and fuel efficiency performance (color), with clear labels and professional styling. The dual encoding reveals patterns like Dodge's high model count but poor efficiency, while Honda balances both aspects well.
:::

## Comparison: All Three Charts

Here's how our treemaps evolved:

| Aspect | Basic | Intermediate | Advanced |
|--------|-------|--------------|----------|
| **Identifiability** | Poor (no labels) | Good (clear labels) | Excellent (labels + data values) |
| **Information Density** | Low (only size) | Medium (size + names) | High (size + efficiency + context) |
| **Color Purpose** | Random distinction | Aesthetic only | Meaningful (efficiency encoding) |
| **Context** | None | Basic title | Full story with insights |
| **Visual Quality** | Basic | Improved | Publication-ready |
| **Data Dimensions** | 1 (count only) | 1 (count only) | 2 (count + efficiency) |

## When to Use Treemaps

::: {.highlight-box .info}
**Treemaps work best for:**

✅ **Showing proportions** - Quickly compare relative sizes of categories

✅ **Hierarchical data** - Display parent-child relationships (we can add subgroups)

✅ **Part-to-whole relationships** - See how individual parts make up a total

✅ **Limited categories** - Work best with 10-20 categories (more becomes cluttered)

✅ **Dual encoding** - Show two variables simultaneously (size + color)

**Avoid treemaps when:**

❌ Precise value comparison is critical (use bar charts)

❌ Data changes over time (use line charts)

❌ Too many small categories (creates tiny, unreadable rectangles)

❌ Negative values are present (treemaps require positive values)
:::

---

## Key Takeaways

::: {.callout .tip}
**Tips for Creating Better Treemaps:**

1. **Always add labels** - Use `geom_treemap_text()` to identify rectangles. Unlabeled treemaps are nearly useless

2. **Use color meaningfully** - Don't just use color for distinction; map it to a second variable (like efficiency, growth rate, or category)

3. **Consider borders** - White borders between rectangles improve clarity and prevent colors from bleeding together

4. **Limit your categories** - If you have too many categories, group smaller ones into "Other" to maintain readability

5. **Use `grow = TRUE`** - This makes text automatically resize to fit rectangles, ensuring readability for all sizes

6. **Choose appropriate color scales**:
   - Sequential (light to dark) for continuous positive values
   - Diverging (red-white-green) when there's a meaningful midpoint
   - Categorical for distinct groups

7. **Add multiple text layers** - Use separate layers for main labels and supporting information (like our count + efficiency example)

8. **Test text contrast** - Ensure text is readable against all background colors. White text with slight transparency often works well

9. **Include a legend** - When color encodes data, always include a properly labeled legend explaining what it represents

10. **Provide context in subtitles** - Don't just show the data; highlight key insights or patterns in your subtitle

11. **Sort your data** - Arrange categories by size (descending) before creating the treemap for better visual organization

12. **Consider hierarchical treemaps** - Use the `subgroup` parameter to create nested treemaps for multi-level hierarchies

:::

## Advanced: Hierarchical Treemap Example

Want to show multiple levels of hierarchy? Here's a bonus example with manufacturers grouped by country:

```{r}
#| label: hierarchical-example
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
#| eval: true

# Add country information (simplified example)
data_hierarchical <- mpg %>%
  mutate(
    country = case_when(
      manufacturer %in% c("audi", "volkswagen") ~ "Germany",
      manufacturer %in% c("toyota", "honda", "nissan", "subaru") ~ "Japan",
      manufacturer %in% c("hyundai") ~ "South Korea",
      TRUE ~ "USA"
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(country, manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(count = n(), avg_hwy = mean(hwy), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(data_hierarchical, aes(
  area = count,
  fill = avg_hwy,
  label = manufacturer,
  subgroup = country                      # Group by country first
)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(          # Add borders around country groups
    colour = "white",
    size = 4
  ) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_text(            # Add country labels
    place = "centre",
    colour = "white",
    alpha = 0.7,
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 16
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(                     # Add manufacturer labels
    colour = "white",
    place = "centre",
    size = 10,
    grow = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",
    mid = "#F4A261",
    high = "#52A675",
    midpoint = 22,
    name = "Avg Highway MPG"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Car Models by Country and Manufacturer",
    subtitle = "Hierarchical view showing country-level groupings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5)
  )
```

## Alternative Packages

While we used `treemapify` in this tutorial, here are other options:

- **`treemap`** - More traditional treemap package with different layout algorithms
- **`d3treeR`** - Interactive treemaps using D3.js (great for Shiny apps!)
- **`plotly`** - Can create interactive treemaps with hover information
